::: {.callout-tip}
## One coherent example

We use six invented shop orders with **distance (km)**, **number of items**, and **fulfilment time (minutes)**. Start the [single-file Python example](../../examples/README.md); this chapter corresponds to `python3 delivery_ml_lab.py linear`.
:::

## The motivating problem

**How can six rows of delivery data become one reusable predictive calculation?**

The feature matrix stores one order per row and one feature per column. Linear systems establish exact constraints, vector spaces define valid combinations, rank determines whether parameters are identifiable, and affine maps add the fixed baseline handling time. A core theme is that the *shape* of a matrix is part of the mathematical contract.

## Central mathematical relationship

$$
X\in\mathbb R^{6\times3},\ \boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^3,\quad \hat{\boldsymbol y}=X\boldsymbol\beta
$$

The equation captures the chapter's principal relationship. Definitions and assumptions are developed in the lessons below; an equation is useful only when the domain and meaning of its symbols are explicit.

## First worked result

For a candidate beta=(3,2,2), an order with distance 1 and 1 item produces 3+2+2=7 minutes. This one expression is evaluated for all six orders by the matrix multiplication X beta.

## What to pay attention to

A column representing distance plus item count is redundant when both original columns are present. Rank—not the number of columns—determines the number of independent parameter directions.

Read the lessons in sequence, reproduce a calculation by hand, then run the related Python demonstration and explain which mathematical claim the output illustrates. A numerical observation is never, by itself, proof of a theorem.
